skills: Counting and sorting fall foods like corn, apples, grapes, and pumpkins
Gratitude talk, naming people and things they are thankful for
Pattern practice on turkey feathers, plaid shirts, and woven baskets
ideas: Print on cardstock, color, and laminate or cover with clear contact paper for a kids' table placemat that wipes clean after dinner.
Have each child write or dictate one thing they're thankful for on the back of the turkey page, then read them aloud before the meal.
In a classroom harvest unit, pair the cornucopia page with a real basket of fruit and let kids match each food to its picture.
Use the Mayflower ship page as a starting point for a short, simple talk about sailing ships and long trips across the ocean.

faq.q: What age are these Thanksgiving coloring pages for?
faq.a: Most pages suit ages 3 to 8. The pumpkin pie and happy Thanksgiving pages have the biggest open shapes for preschoolers, while the cornucopia and dinner table give older kids more small details to fill.

faq.q: Can I print them on cardstock for placemats?
faq.a: Yes. Standard 8.5 x 11 cardstock runs through most home printers. Color with crayons or markers, then laminate or cover with clear contact paper so the placemats survive spills. Set the printer to actual size so the picture fills the page edge to edge.

faq.q: How can I keep kids busy while the turkey cooks?
faq.a: Print a small stack, set out crayons on the kids' table, and add a simple challenge like counting every feather or finding all the corn. A stack of eight pages usually covers a good stretch of cooking time.

skills: Pattern building on ornaments, stockings, and wrapping paper
Comparing sizes by ordering presents from smallest to largest
Storytelling and retelling with Santa, the gingerbread man, and the nativity
ideas: Color the ornament page on cardstock, cut out each ornament, punch a hole, and hang them on the tree with yarn.
Turn the finished stocking page into a name banner by writing each child's name across the fuzzy cuff and stringing the pages together.
Fold a colored page in half to make a handmade Christmas card for grandparents, with a short note written or dictated inside.
In class, read a gingerbread man story first, then color the gingerbread page and have kids retell the ending in their own words.

faq.q: Which Christmas coloring page is easiest for toddlers?
faq.a: The gingerbread man and stocking pages have the largest open shapes and the fewest small details, so they work well for ages 2 to 4 using chunky crayons. Older siblings can pick the ornament or presents pages and add their own wrapping paper designs.

faq.q: Is there a religious Christmas coloring page?
faq.a: Yes. The nativity scene shows Mary, Joseph, baby Jesus in the manger, a sheep, a donkey, and the star. The rest of the set is non-religious, so families can choose what fits their celebration. Many families color the nativity page on Christmas Eve while reading the story aloud.

faq.q: Can I use these for a classroom holiday party?
faq.a: Yes. They are free to print for home and classroom use. Many teachers set out a mix of pages at a coloring station so kids can pick their favorite. Printing on cardstock makes the pages sturdy enough to hang as party decorations afterward.

skills: Building science vocabulary with real dinosaur names and features
Comparing size, shape, and body parts like horns, plates, sails, and clubs
Clapping syllables in long names like stegosaurus and brachiosaurus
ideas: Match each finished page to a dinosaur book or toy figure, and talk about how the picture and the model look the same or different.
Sort the pages into plant eaters and meat eaters as a simple science activity for preschool or kindergarten.
For a dinosaur birthday party, set out the pages with crayons as a quiet table activity while guests arrive.
Hide the colored pages around the room and send kids on a fossil hunt, reading or sounding out each dinosaur name they find.

faq.q: What colors were dinosaurs really?
faq.a: For most dinosaurs, scientists don't know. Skin and feather colors rarely survive in fossils, so kids can use any colors they like and still be right. Scientists sometimes find clues in fossil feathers that hint at dark or striped patterns, so a striped dinosaur is a fair guess too.

faq.q: Are these dinosaur pages good for preschoolers?
faq.a: Yes. The baby dinosaur egg, stegosaurus, and triceratops pages have large shapes for ages 3 to 5. The T. rex jungle and ankylosaurus armor have more details for kids 5 and up. If a page has too much detail for your child, color the dinosaur together and let them finish the background.

faq.q: Which dinosaurs are included?
faq.a: T. rex, triceratops, stegosaurus, spinosaurus, brachiosaurus, velociraptor, ankylosaurus, and a baby dinosaur hatching from an egg. Each page also has its own conversation starters and simple facts to share while coloring.

skills: Using color in order with rainbows, manes, and layered cakes
Imaginative storytelling about castles, clouds, and flying unicorns
Fine motor control while coloring swirls, curls, and spiral horns
ideas: For a unicorn birthday party, print the birthday cake page as an activity and send each guest home with a colored page.
Have kids color the princess and unicorn page, then tell a three-part story about how the two became friends: beginning, middle, and end.
Use the sleepy unicorn on a cloud as a calm bedtime coloring page with soft pastel crayons.
Cut out the unicorn head, glue it to a paper plate, and add yarn for the mane to make a simple craft or mask.

faq.q: What age are these unicorn coloring pages for?
faq.a: Most suit ages 3 to 8. The baby unicorn and rainbow unicorn pages are easier for younger kids, while the unicorn head and castle have more fine detail for older kids. If your child gets tired partway through, a page can easily be finished over two short sittings.

faq.q: What crayons or markers work best for unicorns?
faq.a: Pastel crayons and washable markers look lovely on manes and wings. Gel pens or metallic markers add shine to the horn and stars. Leaving small white spots on the horn and in the eyes makes those parts look shiny without any special supplies.

faq.q: Are these good for a unicorn birthday party?
faq.a: Yes. Print a stack before the party and set them on a table with crayons. The cake page is a natural fit to color while waiting for the real cake. Pair it with a simple game like pin the horn on the unicorn.

skills: Matching and symmetry with mittens and the six-branched snowflake
Size comparison with the snowman's snowballs and the polar bears
Winter science talk about snow, ice, melting, and staying warm
ideas: Color the snowflake page in blues and purples, cut it out, and tape it to a window for a winter display.
Pair the hot cocoa page with a real mug of cocoa on a snow day and talk about steam and melting marshmallows.
In a classroom winter animals unit, use the penguin and polar bear pages to compare where each animal lives.
Freeze a few small toys in a tub of water, color the igloo page while they melt, and talk about how ice changes.

faq.q: Are these winter pages Christmas themed?
faq.a: No. This set focuses on snow, cold weather, and winter animals, so it works from December through February and in classrooms that keep holiday themes separate. Families who celebrate different holidays can all use them together.

faq.q: What age are these winter coloring pages for?
faq.a: The snowman, mittens, and snowflake have bold shapes for ages 3 to 5. The sledding and igloo pages have more details for kids 5 to 8. If a page feels too detailed, let your child color only the main animal or object and leave the background white.

faq.q: How do I make white things like snow stand out?
faq.a: Leave snow areas uncolored, or add a light blue or gray edge. Coloring the sky or background a darker color makes white parts look bright. White crayon over bare paper shows up best if you go over it with a light blue wash or marker afterward.

skills: Counting the eight nights with the menorah's candles
Recognizing shapes like triangles in the Star of David and the dreidel
Learning words and traditions like shamash, sufganiyot, latkes, and gelt
ideas: Color one menorah page each night of Hanukkah, adding one more flame each evening until all eight candles are lit.
Pair the dreidel page with a real dreidel game using chocolate gelt or buttons as playing pieces.
In a classroom winter holidays unit, use these pages alongside a book about Hanukkah to introduce the Festival of Lights.
Make latkes or jelly doughnuts together, then color the matching page while they cool.

faq.q: Why does the menorah have nine candles?
faq.a: Eight candles stand for the eight nights of Hanukkah. The ninth, called the shamash, is the helper candle used to light the others and usually sits higher or in the middle.

faq.q: Are the dreidel faces blank?
faq.a: Yes. The dreidel page has blank sides so kids can draw the Hebrew letters, their own symbols, or simple designs. Kids can also design a whole set of four faces on scrap paper first, then copy their favorite onto the page.

faq.q: What age are these Hanukkah coloring pages for?
faq.a: Most pages suit ages 3 to 8. The Star of David and dreidel have simple shapes for younger kids, and the gelt bag and latkes have more detail for older kids. Younger kids can color one candle or one doughnut at a time over several days.

skills: Early hand control with extra thick outlines and big shapes
Naming colors, shapes, and first letter sounds
Counting small sets like three balloons or five star points
ideas: Use these pages with toddlers and chunky crayons or dot markers for short, low-pressure coloring sessions.
Pick one page a day and connect it to a letter sound, like A for apple, F for fish, and B for butterfly.
Tape a page to the wall or an easel so kids color standing up, which uses shoulder and arm muscles.
Use the easy house page for a family drawing game: kids color it, then add people, pets, or a garden.

faq.q: What age are simple coloring pages for?
faq.a: These pages are made for ages 2 to 5, with extra thick outlines and large open spaces that are easier for little hands to color. Some older kids with emerging hand control also enjoy them as a quick win.

faq.q: What should toddlers color with?
faq.a: Chunky crayons, washable markers, and dot markers work well for young kids. Short crayon pieces can also encourage a more mature grip. Holding a short crayon piece makes it harder to grab with a whole fist.

faq.q: Is it okay if my child scribbles outside the lines?
faq.a: Yes. Scribbling is a normal part of learning to color, and many kids stay inside lines more often as their hand control grows. If you have concerns, ask your child's teacher or pediatrician.

skills: Learning names and jobs of community vehicles
Counting wheels, windows, and ladder rungs
Talking about safety with fire trucks, police cars, and school buses
ideas: Take a walk around the neighborhood and look for the vehicles on these pages, coloring each one after you see it.
In a community helpers unit, pair the fire truck, police car, garbage truck, and school bus with the people who drive them.
Line up the colored pages and sort them into vehicles that carry people and vehicles that carry things.
Write a number on the race car's side and use the page for a counting game with toy cars.

faq.q: What age are these car and truck coloring pages for?
faq.a: Most suit ages 3 to 8. The police car and tractor have bigger, simpler shapes for preschoolers, and the fire truck and garbage truck have more parts for older kids. Kids who love vehicles may want to color the whole set and staple it into a little truck book.

faq.q: Which vehicles are included?
faq.a: A race car, fire truck, dump truck, police car, school bus, tractor, monster truck, and garbage truck. Each page also lists simple facts about what that vehicle does, so you can talk about it while coloring.

faq.q: How can I use these for a vehicle-themed party?
faq.a: Print a stack, set out crayons, and let kids pick their favorite truck. Many kids enjoy writing their age or initial on the race car's number circle. A garbage truck or fire truck page also makes a nice thank-you to give the real workers in your neighborhood.

skills: Number recognition with the clock, the countdown, and the year 2027
Setting simple goals and putting ideas into words
Pattern practice with party hats, confetti, and balloons
ideas: Color the goals page together on New Year's Day, hang it on the fridge, and check in on progress at the end of each month.
Use the countdown rocket page to practice counting backward from 10 before the family's early countdown.
Set up a noon year's eve party for little ones, with these pages at a table and a countdown to 12 o'clock noon.
In class, use the midnight clock page to introduce the hour and minute hands before a time-telling lesson.

faq.q: What age is the goals page for?
faq.a: Most kids ages 4 to 8 can choose three simple goals. Younger kids can draw pictures inside the stars, and older kids can write words. Keep the goals small and specific, like helping set the table or reading a book every night.

faq.q: Are these good for a noon year's eve party?
faq.a: Yes. Many families and classrooms celebrate at noon with little ones, and the clock and countdown pages fit that idea. Counting down to noon lets young kids join in without staying up late.

faq.q: Will the 2027 page be updated?
faq.a: The 2027 page is made for the coming year. The other pages in the set have no year on them and can be used every New Year. Families can save each year's goals page to look back on together.

skills: Recognizing heart shapes and comparing big and small
Writing names and short notes for friends and family
Talking about kindness, friendship, and showing love
ideas: Color the be my valentine page, fold it in half, and write a short note inside to make a handmade card.
In class, give each student a different page to color and swap with a friend at a Valentine's party.
Cut out the big heart page, punch holes around the edge, and lace yarn through for a sewing card.
Use the mailbox page as a cover for a paper bag mailbox to hold valentines from classmates.

faq.q: What age are these Valentine's Day coloring pages for?
faq.a: Most suit ages 3 to 8. The big heart page is the easiest for toddlers, while the love bugs and mailbox pages have more small details. Toddlers can also use dot markers inside the hearts for an easy first coloring activity.

faq.q: Can I use these as Valentine's cards?
faq.a: Yes. Print them on cardstock, color them, and fold or trim them into cards. Kids can write their name or a short message on the back. Glue the colored page onto folded construction paper for a sturdier card.

faq.q: Do you have non-romantic Valentine's pages for school?
faq.a: Yes. The dinosaur, puppy, teddy bear, and love bugs pages focus on friendship and kindness, which suits classroom parties. Check your school's policy on candy and cards, since it can vary by classroom, and plan the swap to include everyone.

skills: Counting leaves on shamrocks and four-leaf clovers
Naming rainbow colors in order
Early engineering talk about how a leprechaun trap works
ideas: Color the leprechaun trap page first, then build a real trap from a shoebox, a stick, and some gold coins.
Go on a clover hunt outside, then color the shamrock and four-leaf clover pages and count the leaves on each.
In class, hang the rainbow pages in a row along a wall with a pot of gold at the end.
Read a book about leprechauns, then color the leprechaun page and have kids write or dictate what they would wish for.

faq.q: What age are these St. Patrick's Day coloring pages for?
faq.a: Most suit ages 3 to 8. The shamrock and four-leaf clover have big, simple shapes for toddlers, and the leprechaun and trap pages have more detail. Younger kids can color the big shamrock while older siblings fill in the leprechaun's buckles and coins.

faq.q: When is St. Patrick's Day?
faq.a: St. Patrick's Day is celebrated every year on March 17. Many schools mark the day with green clothing, crafts, and a leprechaun hunt.

faq.q: Can I use the trap page for a classroom STEM project?
faq.a: Yes. Many classes color the trap page as a plan, then build a trap from cardboard, tape, and craft supplies. Kids can label the parts of their plan, like the bait, the ladder, and the trigger stick, before building.

skills: Spotting and repeating patterns like zigzags, dots, and stripes
Visual scanning to find hidden eggs
Learning spring words like chick, lamb, bloom, and hatch
ideas: Color the egg hunt page before a real egg hunt and count how many eggs are hidden in the picture.
Cut out the colored egg and basket pages and use them to decorate the Easter table or a spring bulletin board.
Pair the baby chick page with a book about how chicks hatch from eggs for a simple spring science lesson.
Have kids design their own egg patterns on the blank parts of the egg page, then decorate real eggs to match.

faq.q: What age are these Easter coloring pages for?
faq.a: Most suit ages 3 to 8. The big Easter egg and baby chick have large shapes for younger kids, and the egg hunt scene has more detail for older kids. Toddlers can color the big egg with dot markers or chunky crayons.

faq.q: Is there a religious Easter coloring page?
faq.a: Yes. The cross and lilies page is a Christian Easter image. The rest of the set focuses on spring, bunnies, chicks, and eggs. Families can choose the pages that fit how they celebrate.

faq.q: Can I use these pages for a spring classroom unit?
faq.a: Yes. The lamb, chick, and egg pages fit a spring or life cycle unit even outside of Easter. The bunny painting eggs page also works well before an egg dyeing activity.

turkey-coloring-page.talkAbout: Male turkeys, called toms, are the ones that puff up and fan their tail feathers like this to show off. Wild turkeys can fly short distances and often sleep up in trees at night, which surprises a lot of kids. Ask your child what sound a turkey makes, then see who in the family can do the best gobble.
turkey-coloring-page.colorTips: Give each tail feather its own fall shade, or alternate red, orange, and brown all the way around the fan for an easy pattern. Older kids can add stripes or dots inside every feather, then color the fallen leaves at the turkey's feet in matching colors. The red wattle under the beak is a fun little detail to point out and color last.
turkey-coloring-page.learning: Counting the tail feathers out loud before coloring, then again after, is simple one-to-one counting practice that feels like part of the fun.

cute-turkey-coloring-page.talkAbout: This little turkey is hugging an ear of corn, a crop people grew in the Americas long before the first Thanksgiving feast. Corn kernels grow in neat rows around the cob, and one special kind of corn pops into popcorn when it gets hot. Talk about which Thanksgiving foods your child likes best and which ones they haven't tried yet. Baby turkeys are called poults, a new word most grown-ups don't know either.
cute-turkey-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the kernels sunny yellow, or mix red, purple, and gold like the speckled corn people hang on doors in the fall. The square buckle on the hat looks sharp in gold or gray, and the wide striped tail feathers are made for an alternating color pattern.
cute-turkey-coloring-page.learning: The tall hat, the square buckle, and the round body make it easy to stop and name shapes like circles, squares, and rectangles as your child colors.

pumpkin-pie-coloring-page.talkAbout: Pumpkins are a type of squash, and they grow on long vines that spread across the ground. Pumpkin pie gets its warm, cozy flavor from spices like cinnamon, nutmeg, and ginger. Ask your child what they would put on top of their slice, and whether whipped cream wins over ice cream. Most pumpkins turn orange in the fall, but some kinds are white, green, or even blue-gray.
pumpkin-pie-coloring-page.colorTips: A soft orange or tan works well for the filling, with golden brown around the wavy crust edge. Leave the whipped cream swirl white or give it a light gray shadow, and let older kids make the pie server shiny with silver and a wooden brown handle.
pumpkin-pie-coloring-page.learning: Imagine cutting the pie into two halves, then four quarters, and draw light pencil lines to show it, a friendly first look at fractions.

cornucopia-coloring-page.talkAbout: A cornucopia is also called a horn of plenty, and it stands for a big, happy harvest. Point to each food and name it together: apples, pears, grapes, corn, and one small pumpkin. Then talk about where each one grows, since apples and pears hang on trees, grapes grow on vines, and corn grows on tall stalks.
cornucopia-coloring-page.colorTips: Use tan and brown for the woven horn, then give each fruit and vegetable its real-life color for a quick matching lesson. Older kids can color every other strip of the weave a darker brown so the basket texture really stands out. Leaves tucked between the fruit can be green, red, or gold.
cornucopia-coloring-page.learning: Each grape is a small circle, so coloring the bunches one grape at a time builds fine motor control, and counting them turns it into math.

happy-thanksgiving-coloring-page.talkAbout: In the United States, Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November, and Canada celebrates its own Thanksgiving in October. It's a day for sharing a meal and saying what we are grateful for. Ask your child to name one person and one thing they feel thankful for this year, and write their answers on the back of the page.
happy-thanksgiving-coloring-page.colorTips: Bubble letters are fun to fill with one color each, or with stripes and polka dots for older kids who want a challenge. Color the pumpkin orange with a green stem, and try red on one oak leaf and gold on the other. Count the letters in each word before starting, so your child knows how many bubble letters are ahead.
happy-thanksgiving-coloring-page.learning: Point to the H, T, and G, say each letter's sound together, and then spell THANKS out loud one letter at a time.

thanksgiving-dinner-coloring-page.talkAbout: Name every food on this table together: a roast turkey, a bowl of mashed potatoes, an ear of corn, and a pie for dessert. Mashed potatoes start out as potatoes that grow underground, then get boiled and mashed until they're soft. Ask your child which food they'd put on their plate first and which they'd save for last. Talk about who sets the table at your house and what jobs a small helper could take on.
thanksgiving-dinner-coloring-page.colorTips: Golden brown works for the roast turkey, with red and green for the little garnish around the platter. The two chairs can be a warm wood color, and kids can add a tablecloth pattern of stripes or checks across the table.
thanksgiving-dinner-coloring-page.learning: Describing each food as hot, cold, sweet, crunchy, or soft is easy vocabulary building that kids can use at the real dinner table.

scarecrow-coloring-page.talkAbout: Farmers have used scarecrows for a very long time to keep hungry birds away from their crops. The crow sitting on this scarecrow's arm doesn't look scared at all, which makes for a funny conversation. Ask your child what they would use to build a scarecrow at home, from old clothes to a hat for the top. Point out the straw poking out of the sleeves and hat, since straw is what a scarecrow is usually stuffed with.
scarecrow-coloring-page.colorTips: Try a plaid pattern on the shirt, blue on the overalls, and a different bright color on each patch. The corn stalks look great in green and gold, and the crow can stay black or become any bird your child likes.
scarecrow-coloring-page.learning: Counting the patches on the overalls and the corn plants on each side of the scarecrow mixes counting with careful looking.

mayflower-ship-coloring-page.talkAbout: The Mayflower was a sailing ship that carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic Ocean to North America in 1620. The trip took about two months, with more than a hundred passengers crowded on board. Sailing ships move when wind fills their sails, so talk about what might happen on a calm day with no wind at all.
mayflower-ship-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the ocean in layers of light and dark blue, then use wood browns for the hull and masts. Older kids can add stripes to the sails or design small flags for the tops of the masts, and the seagulls can stay white with gray wing tips. A pale sky blue behind the gulls makes the white sails pop.
mayflower-ship-coloring-page.learning: Counting the three sails and the windows along the hull, then comparing the tall middle sail with the shorter ones, builds counting and size words.

santa-claus-coloring-page.talkAbout: Santa's story grew from a real man, Saint Nicholas, who was remembered for kindness and secret gift giving. Around the world he goes by other names too, like Father Christmas in England and Père Noël in France. Ask your child what they think is wrapped in the presents peeking out of Santa's sack. Talk about places Santa might visit, from snowy towns to warm beaches where it is summer in December.
santa-claus-coloring-page.colorTips: A red suit, white fluffy trim, and a black belt with a gold buckle give the classic look. Let kids pick bright wrapping colors for the gifts in the sack, and older kids can add tiny stripes or dots to each one.
santa-claus-coloring-page.learning: Santa's waving hand makes a good moment to practice left and right: ask which hand he is waving, then have your child wave the same one.

christmas-tree-coloring-page.talkAbout: Evergreen trees like firs and pines keep their needles all winter, which is one reason people bring them indoors during the coldest part of the year. Many families top their tree with a star or an angel. Talk about how your family decorates and which ornament is your child's favorite.
christmas-tree-coloring-page.colorTips: Use green for the branches, then give each round ornament a different color. Older kids can turn the bead garland into a repeating pattern like red, gold, red, gold, and the three gifts underneath can each get their own wrapping paper. Yellow or gold on the star at the top gives the whole page a finished look.
christmas-tree-coloring-page.learning: Counting the ornaments row by row from the star down to the gifts is natural counting practice, and it shows how the rows get wider toward the bottom.

reindeer-coloring-page.talkAbout: Reindeer live in cold northern places, and they are the only kind of deer where both males and females usually grow antlers. Their wide hooves work a bit like snowshoes so they don't sink into deep snow. Point out the jingle bells on this reindeer's collar, then listen for real bell sounds around town this season. In parts of the far north, people have herded reindeer for a very long time, using them for milk, travel, and warm hides.
reindeer-coloring-page.colorTips: Brown and tan work well for the fur, with a lighter shade on the belly, muzzle, and inside of the ears. Make the antlers a darker brown, and give the jingle bells a shiny gold or silver.
reindeer-coloring-page.learning: Reindeer starts with R, so trace an R in the air together and think of other R words like red, run, and ribbon.

gingerbread-man-coloring-page.talkAbout: Gingerbread cookies get their name and their spicy taste from ginger, a root that grows underground. People have baked shaped gingerbread for hundreds of years, and many families still make it every December. Talk about the old story where the gingerbread man runs away, and ask how your child thinks it ends.
gingerbread-man-coloring-page.colorTips: Light brown makes the cookie look freshly baked, and the icing zigzags on the arms and legs can stay white. Give the three gumdrop buttons three different colors, and swirl red and white on the peppermint beside him. For a pattern challenge, older kids can draw extra icing details like a bow tie or a smile on the hands and feet.
gingerbread-man-coloring-page.learning: Tracing the wavy icing lines with a fingertip before coloring is good warm-up for the up-and-down strokes kids use in early writing.

christmas-ornament-coloring-page.talkAbout: Glass ornaments first became popular on Christmas trees in Germany, and the idea spread around the world from there. Look at the three ornaments together: one has stars, one has stripes, and one has dots. Ask your child which one they would hang right at the front of the tree.
christmas-ornament-coloring-page.colorTips: This page is made for patterns, so color the stripes in alternating colors, give each star a different shade, and make the dots a rainbow. Don't forget the bows and ribbons at the top, which can match the ornament below each one. A metallic gel pen or glitter glue on a few stars makes the page sparkle when it hangs in a window.
christmas-ornament-coloring-page.learning: Naming stars, stripes, and dots and then building a simple AB color pattern on one ornament is early pattern thinking, a building block of math.

christmas-stocking-coloring-page.talkAbout: Hanging stockings is a tradition in many homes, and the custom is often linked to stories of Saint Nicholas leaving small gifts. Look at what is peeking out of this one: a candy cane and a little teddy bear. Ask your child what small surprise they would hope to find in their own stocking.
christmas-stocking-coloring-page.colorTips: Red with a white fuzzy cuff is the classic choice, but stripes, plaid, or polka dots make it one of a kind. The candy cane gets red and white stripes, and the teddy bear can be brown, tan, or any color your child picks. Color the heel and toe a different shade from the rest of the stocking for a classic knitted look.
christmas-stocking-coloring-page.learning: Writing or tracing their own name across the wide cuff turns this page into real name practice that kids love to hang up.

christmas-presents-coloring-page.talkAbout: Count the boxes together, then talk about which present is the biggest and which is the smallest. Giving gifts is one way to show people we care, and a handmade drawing can be a gift too. Ask who your child would like to give this finished page to, and help them write a short note on the back. You might also chat about gifts that don't come in boxes, like helping, sharing, or spending time together.
christmas-presents-coloring-page.colorTips: Choose a different wrapping color for each box and a contrasting color for every bow. Older kids can design their own wrapping paper inside the boxes with stars, stripes, or tiny trees. Leave a small tag on one box blank so your child can write a name.
christmas-presents-coloring-page.learning: Putting the four presents in order from smallest to largest is hands-on practice with size comparison and ordering.

nativity-scene-coloring-page.talkAbout: This scene shows the Christmas story of Jesus born in a stable, with Mary and Joseph beside the manger. A manger is a feeding box for animals, filled here with soft hay. Point to the sheep, the donkey, and the bright star above the stable, and talk about the part the star plays in the story.
nativity-scene-coloring-page.colorTips: Warm browns for the wooden stable and golden yellow for the hay and star make the whole scene glow. Mary is often shown in blue, Joseph in brown, and the sheep and donkey can be soft white and gray. Older kids can color the star's light rays in pale yellow, then shade the stable roof in two browns to show the wooden boards.
nativity-scene-coloring-page.learning: Naming each person and animal, then retelling the story in order, builds listening and retelling skills.

t-rex-coloring-page.talkAbout: Tyrannosaurus rex lived in what is now western North America and had huge jaws filled with banana-sized teeth. Its arms were short but strong, with just two fingers on each hand. Its name means "tyrant lizard king," which kids usually love to say in a big, booming voice.
t-rex-coloring-page.colorTips: Scientists don't know the true colors of most dinosaurs, so any color is fair game. Try green with a lighter belly for the T. rex, then use orange and red on the volcano and two shades of green on the palm leaves. A pattern of darker stripes down the back makes this friendly T. rex look even bolder.
t-rex-coloring-page.learning: T. rex starts with T, so practice the T sound and hunt for other T words in the picture, like tree, teeth, and tail.

triceratops-coloring-page.talkAbout: Triceratops means "three-horned face," and this one is happily munching leaves because it was a plant eater. The big bony frill around its neck may have helped it show off or recognize others of its kind. It lived at the same time as T. rex, so the two may have crossed paths. Its beak-like mouth worked well for snipping tough plants, a bit like a parrot's beak.
triceratops-coloring-page.colorTips: The frill is the best spot for a pattern, so try stripes, spots, or a fan of rainbow colors. Color the three horns a pale ivory or tan, and use a few different greens on the leafy bush. A light brown under the feet grounds the picture.
triceratops-coloring-page.learning: Counting the three horns ties right into the name, since tri means three, just like in triangle and tricycle.

stegosaurus-coloring-page.talkAbout: Stegosaurus had large plates standing up along its back and sharp spikes at the end of its tail. Its head was tiny compared with its big body, and it ate plants. It lived so long ago that T. rex actually lived closer in time to people than to Stegosaurus, which makes for a fun dinner fact.
stegosaurus-coloring-page.colorTips: Alternate two colors along the back plates, like orange and yellow, for an easy pattern. Make the tail spikes a darker shade, and use the small grass tufts for careful coloring practice. Older kids can draw thin lines inside each plate, like veins in a leaf, and color between them.
stegosaurus-coloring-page.learning: Counting the back plates from head to tail is simple counting practice, and you can point out which plates are big and which are small along the way.

spinosaurus-coloring-page.talkAbout: Spinosaurus had a tall sail on its back and a long, narrow snout a bit like a crocodile's. It spent a lot of time in and near rivers and caught fish, just like the one in this picture. It was one of the longest meat-eating dinosaurs scientists have found.
spinosaurus-coloring-page.colorTips: The sail looks striking with stripes running up it in sunset colors like red, orange, and yellow. Color the river in layers of blue, and make the fish and splashing water drops silver or light blue. Older kids can add small ripples around its legs to show the water moving.
spinosaurus-coloring-page.learning: Talk about the word splash and the hissing S sound it starts with, then count the water drops falling from the fish together. You can also compare the long snout with the short tail of the fish.

brachiosaurus-coloring-page.talkAbout: Brachiosaurus had a very long neck, and its front legs were longer than its back legs, so it stood tall like a giraffe. That height helped it reach leaves high in the trees, just like in this picture. It was a plant eater and one of the biggest animals ever to walk on land. Ask your child to stretch up as tall as they can and pretend to munch leaves like a brachiosaurus.
brachiosaurus-coloring-page.colorTips: Soft gray, green, or blue suit the long body, and older kids can add darker spots or stripes down the neck. The tree, bushes, and hill behind give plenty of room for different greens and browns.
brachiosaurus-coloring-page.learning: Comparing the dinosaur, the tree, and the small bushes is an easy way to practice size words like tall, taller, short, and shorter.

velociraptor-coloring-page.talkAbout: Velociraptor was about the size of a turkey, much smaller than the ones in movies. Fossils show it had feathers, and it had a curved claw on each foot. It ran on two legs and was likely quick on its feet. Its name means "swift thief," a fun fact that fits the running pose in this picture. Many scientists see dinosaurs like this one as close relatives of today's birds, so ask your child which birds it reminds them of.
velociraptor-coloring-page.colorTips: Since velociraptor had feathers, kids can make the arm feathers bright like a bird's, in blue, green, or red. Add stripes along the back and tail as a pattern challenge for older kids. Leave the long curved claw on each foot a pale gray so kids can find it easily.
velociraptor-coloring-page.learning: Velociraptor is a long word, so clap out its syllables together, ve-lo-ci-rap-tor, and count the claps.

ankylosaurus-coloring-page.talkAbout: Ankylosaurus was covered in bony armor plates, almost like a living tank. The big club at the end of its tail was made of solid bone and was probably swung to protect itself. It was a plant eater that munched on low-growing plants like the ferns around it here.
ankylosaurus-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the armor plates in a checkerboard of two colors, or give each plate its own shade of brown or green. The tail club can be darker than the body, and the feathery ferns look great in two shades of green. Use a lighter color for the belly and face so the armor on top stands out.
ankylosaurus-coloring-page.learning: Most of the armor plates are rounded squares, so name the shape as you color each one and count how many fit in a single row.

baby-dinosaur-egg-coloring-page.talkAbout: Dinosaurs hatched from eggs, just like birds and turtles do today. Scientists have found fossil nests with dinosaur eggs still inside them. Make a list together of other animals that hatch from eggs, from chickens to crocodiles. Ask your child what kind of dinosaur this baby might grow up to be and what name they would give it. Some fossil eggs are small enough to hold in one hand, though the dinosaurs that hatched from them grew to be enormous.
baby-dinosaur-egg-coloring-page.colorTips: Give the baby dinosaur a bright color and the egg a soft cream with speckles. The sticks in the nest are good for practicing coloring in one direction, along the length of each stick.
baby-dinosaur-egg-coloring-page.learning: Telling what happens first, next, and last as an egg hatches gives kids practice with sequence words they will use in storytelling.

rainbow-unicorn-coloring-page.talkAbout: Unicorns are imaginary animals that show up in old stories and legends from many parts of the world. Rainbows, on the other hand, are real: they appear when sunlight shines through raindrops and splits into colors. Ask your child what this unicorn might find at the end of its rainbow, and let the story grow from there.
rainbow-unicorn-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the rainbow bands in order from the top: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple. The unicorn's mane and tail can pick up a few of those same colors, and the clouds at each end can stay white with a pale gray edge.
rainbow-unicorn-coloring-page.learning: Saying the rainbow colors in order, top band to bottom, is color-word practice and a simple first lesson in sequencing. Counting the bumps on each fluffy cloud adds a quick number task.

winged-unicorn-coloring-page.talkAbout: A horse with wings in old Greek stories is called Pegasus, and a unicorn with wings like this one is sometimes called an alicorn. Birds fly by flapping strong wings covered in feathers, and these wings have feathers drawn in rows. Ask your child where they would go if they could ride a flying unicorn for one night.
winged-unicorn-coloring-page.colorTips: The feathered wings are the best spot for color, so try fading from pink at the top to purple at the tips, or give each row of feathers its own shade. A dark blue night sky around the white stars makes the page feel magical, and the hill below can be a deep green.
winged-unicorn-coloring-page.learning: Counting the stars in the sky, then counting the rows of feathers on one wing, gives kids two counting jobs in one picture.

baby-unicorn-coloring-page.talkAbout: A baby horse is called a foal, so some people call a baby unicorn a foal too. This little one is sitting in a patch of flowers with big, sparkly eyes and a tiny horn. Talk about other baby animal names your child knows, like puppy, kitten, calf, and chick. Ask your child what name they would give this baby unicorn and what it likes to eat.
baby-unicorn-coloring-page.colorTips: Soft pastels like light pink, mint, and lavender suit this baby unicorn, with a brighter color for the mane. The flowers around it are a great place for variety, and older kids can make every flower a different color with a yellow center. Leave the white sparkle spots in the big eyes uncolored so they shine.
baby-unicorn-coloring-page.learning: Counting the flowers and naming the flower parts, like petals, center, and stem, builds early science vocabulary.

unicorn-head-coloring-page.talkAbout: In old stories, a unicorn's horn was said to have special powers, like making water clean to drink. This unicorn wears a crown of flowers in its flowing mane. Ask your child which real flowers they would use to make a flower crown, and look for some on your next walk.
unicorn-head-coloring-page.colorTips: The long, swirly mane is perfect for stripes of color that follow each curl, like pink, purple, and blue. Color the spiral horn gold or silver, and give each flower in the crown its own bright shade with green leaves between them.
unicorn-head-coloring-page.learning: Tracing the swirl on the horn with a finger from bottom to top is good practice for the curved strokes used in writing letters like S and C. Counting the flowers in the crown is a nice extra task.

princess-and-unicorn-coloring-page.talkAbout: This princess is gently petting the unicorn, which is a nice way to talk about being kind and gentle with animals. Real horses like a calm, slow touch on their neck, and they can startle at sudden noises. Ask your child to tell a short story about how the princess and the unicorn became friends.
princess-and-unicorn-coloring-page.colorTips: Let your child design the princess gown in any color, with a gold or silver crown on top. The unicorn's mane and tail can match the gown, and the flowers in the meadow add small pops of color at the bottom of the page.
princess-and-unicorn-coloring-page.learning: Making up a story with a beginning, a middle, and an end about these two friends is early storytelling practice. Retelling the story the next day helps kids remember details too.

unicorn-castle-coloring-page.talkAbout: Real castles were built long ago, often of stone, with tall towers so guards could watch the land around them. This fairy tale castle has three towers with pointed roofs and flags on top. Ask your child who lives inside the castle and what the unicorn is doing standing on the path outside. Some real castles, like ones in Germany and Scotland, still stand today and families can visit them.
unicorn-castle-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the castle walls light gray or pink, then give each pointed roof a different bright color. The winding path can be tan or stepping-stone gray, and the flags on top are small enough for a fine-tip marker challenge.
unicorn-castle-coloring-page.learning: The castle has triangle roofs, rectangle towers, and an arched door, so it's a great page for naming shapes and counting the three towers.

unicorn-on-cloud-coloring-page.talkAbout: The moon in this picture is a crescent, the thin curved shape we see on some nights as the moon changes. The moon doesn't make its own light; it reflects light from the sun. This sleepy unicorn makes a calm bedtime page, so talk about what helps your child wind down at night.
unicorn-on-cloud-coloring-page.colorTips: Soft, sleepy colors work well here: lavender, light blue, and pale pink on the unicorn, with a white or pale gray cloud. Color the moon and stars yellow, and older kids can shade the whole background in dark blue for a night sky.
unicorn-on-cloud-coloring-page.learning: Talking about day and night, and what we see in the sky at each time, is a gentle science conversation for bedtime. Counting the stars around the moon before bed is a calm way to end the day.

unicorn-birthday-cake-coloring-page.talkAbout: This three-layer cake has a unicorn horn and ears on top, a popular design for birthday parties. Many families sing a birthday song and make a wish before blowing out the candles. Ask your child what flavor of cake they would choose and what they might wish for.
unicorn-birthday-cake-coloring-page.colorTips: Make each layer of frosting a different pastel, and color the sprinkles in a rainbow of tiny dots. The horn can be gold, the ears pink inside, and each candle can get its own stripes with a yellow flame.
unicorn-birthday-cake-coloring-page.learning: Counting the three layers and the candles on top, then talking about how many candles your child had on their last birthday, makes this a counting page. Comparing the widest bottom layer with the smallest top layer adds size words like wide and narrow.

snowman-coloring-page.talkAbout: This snowman is built from three snowballs stacked from biggest at the bottom to smallest on top. Packing snow works best when it is a little wet and near freezing, which is why fluffy powder falls apart in your hands. Ask your child what would happen to this snowman on a warm, sunny day, and talk about melting.
snowman-coloring-page.colorTips: Leave the snowman white or give him a pale blue shadow on one side, then go bold on the scarf with stripes. Orange for the carrot nose, brown for the stick arms, and black for the hat finish the classic look, though a purple top hat is just as fun.
snowman-coloring-page.learning: Lining up the three snowballs by size, from small to big, is easy practice with comparing and ordering, and counting the buttons down the front adds a quick number job.

mittens-coloring-page.talkAbout: Mittens keep fingers warmer than gloves because the fingers stay together and share their heat. This pair is joined by a string, a trick that keeps one mitten from getting lost. Ask your child what else they wear to stay warm, from hats to boots, and get dressed for the snow in pretend play.
mittens-coloring-page.colorTips: This is a matching page, so color both mittens exactly the same: same stripes, same cuff, same snowflake. Older kids can try a different pattern on each cuff, then add a color to the twisty string connecting them. The snowflakes on the backs of the mittens can be white on a colored background, which means coloring carefully around them.
mittens-coloring-page.learning: Making the two mittens match builds careful looking and the idea of a pair, a word to connect to socks, shoes, and boots.

penguin-coloring-page.talkAbout: Penguins are birds that can't fly, but they are excellent swimmers and use their flippers like wings underwater. Almost all penguins live in the southern half of the world, and some kinds live where it is warm. This one has a fish beside it, a favorite food for penguins. Emperor penguins are the tallest kind, and the fathers keep the egg warm on their feet.
penguin-coloring-page.colorTips: Black or dark blue for the back and white for the belly matches real penguins, with orange for the beak and feet. The knit hat is where kids can go wild with stripes and a bright pom-pom, and the ice floe can be pale blue.
penguin-coloring-page.learning: Penguin starts with P, so practice the P sound by popping your lips and listing P words like pom-pom, play, and puddle.

polar-bear-coloring-page.talkAbout: Polar bears live in the icy Arctic, and their thick fur and a layer of fat keep them warm. Under their white-looking fur, their skin is black, which surprises most kids. A mother polar bear usually stays close to her cubs for about two years while they learn to hunt and swim.
polar-bear-coloring-page.colorTips: White crayon doesn't show up much, so try a very light cream, pale gray, or soft blue shading on the fur. Color the noses and eyes black, and use pale blues and grays for the ice hill and snow. Older kids can draw a few snowflakes falling around the bears and color the sky behind them a soft blue.
polar-bear-coloring-page.learning: Talk about big and little by comparing the mother bear and her cub, then find other big and little pairs around the room.

snowflake-coloring-page.talkAbout: Snowflakes form high in the clouds when tiny water droplets freeze into ice crystals. Most snowflakes have six sides or six branches, just like this big one. The next time it snows, catch a few on a dark mitten or coat and look closely before they melt. Snowflakes come in many shapes, from flat stars to tiny columns, depending on how cold and damp the air is.
snowflake-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the snowflake in icy blues and purples, or make every branch a different color. For a pattern challenge, repeat the same colors on all six branches so the flake stays balanced. Big open shapes like these are great for little hands using chunky crayons or dot markers. Cut the finished snowflake out and tape it to a window for a wintry display.
snowflake-coloring-page.learning: Counting the six branches and noticing that each branch looks the same is a gentle first look at symmetry.

sledding-coloring-page.talkAbout: Sleds slide easily on snow because they have smooth runners and very little to catch on. Gravity pulls the sled down the hill, which is why you have to walk back up again. Ask your child what makes sledding fun and what helps keep everyone safe, like going feet first and watching for trees.
sledding-coloring-page.colorTips: Choose a bright coat and hat so the child stands out against the white snow. The sled can be red or wooden brown, and the pine tree looks great in a deep green with a little white snow left on its branches. Older kids can add tracks behind the sled to show where it has been.
sledding-coloring-page.learning: Words like up, down, fast, and slow come up naturally when you talk about this picture, and they build position and speed vocabulary.

hot-cocoa-coloring-page.talkAbout: Hot cocoa is made from cocoa powder, which comes from the beans of the cacao tree. Cacao trees grow in warm places near the equator, a long way from the snow. Talk about what your child likes in their mug, and blow on a pretend cup together to cool it down. Steam rises from hot drinks because warm water turns into a gas and floats up, which is what the swirls above the mug show.
hot-cocoa-coloring-page.colorTips: Brown for the cocoa and white or pastel pink for the marshmallows makes it look cozy. The mug is the star, so add stripes, dots, or a color around the heart, and give the cookie dark brown chocolate chips. Color the steam swirls a soft gray or leave them white.
hot-cocoa-coloring-page.learning: Counting the marshmallows and the chocolate chips on the cookie gives two quick counting jobs on one page.

igloo-coloring-page.talkAbout: Igloos are traditional snow shelters built by Inuit people in the Arctic, made from blocks of packed snow. Snow traps air, so it works like a blanket and holds warmth inside. The husky sitting out front is a kind of dog bred to pull sleds through cold, snowy places. Ask your child how many snow blocks they think it took to build the whole dome, then count one row together to check.
igloo-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the snow blocks in very light blue, or alternate pale blue and white for a brick-like pattern. Give the husky gray and white fur and blue or brown eyes, and leave the doorway dark so it looks like a real entrance. Pale blue snow on the ground ties the scene together.
igloo-coloring-page.learning: The igloo is a half circle, or dome, and each block is a rectangle, so it's a natural spot to name and trace shapes.

menorah-coloring-page.talkAbout: A Hanukkah menorah, also called a hanukkiah, holds nine candles. Eight stand for the eight nights of Hanukkah, and the raised helper candle in the middle is called the shamash, which is used to light the others. One more candle is lit each night until all eight are glowing on the last night. Families often place the lit menorah in a window so people passing by can see the lights.
menorah-coloring-page.colorTips: Gold, silver, or bright blue look lovely for the menorah base and branches. Color each flame yellow with an orange center, and older kids can give the candles a repeating pattern of blue and white.
menorah-coloring-page.learning: Counting the candles to nine, then pointing out that the shamash sits higher than the rest, is simple counting plus position words like middle and higher.

dreidel-coloring-page.talkAbout: A dreidel is a four-sided spinning top used in a game played during Hanukkah. Each side has a Hebrew letter, and the letter it lands on tells you whether you take or give coins or candy. The faces on this dreidel are blank, so your child can draw letters, symbols, or their own designs on each side.
dreidel-coloring-page.colorTips: Give each visible face its own color, like blue, white, and silver, then color the handle on top. The curved motion lines can be a lighter shade so the dreidel looks like it's spinning.
dreidel-coloring-page.learning: Talk about the dreidel as a shape with flat sides and a point, and count the sides you can see compared with the four it really has. Spinning a real dreidel or a small top after coloring is a hands-on way to talk about balance and motion.

star-of-david-coloring-page.talkAbout: The Star of David is a symbol of the Jewish people and appears on the flag of Israel. It has six points and is made from two triangles laid over each other, one pointing up and one pointing down. Trace each triangle with a finger to find them. Some families hang the star in a window or wear it on a necklace.
star-of-david-coloring-page.colorTips: Blue and white are traditional colors for the star, and the sparkles around it can be gold or silver. Older kids can color each small triangle around the edge a different shade and leave the center hexagon a solid color. For an easy version, color the whole star blue and leave the background white.
star-of-david-coloring-page.learning: This page is full of triangles, so count the small triangles around the outside and name the six-sided shape in the middle, a hexagon.

jelly-doughnut-coloring-page.talkAbout: Jelly doughnuts are called sufganiyot in Hebrew, and they are a favorite Hanukkah treat. Foods fried in oil are eaten during Hanukkah to remember the story of a small amount of oil that lasted eight nights. Ask your child what jelly flavor they would choose for the middle. Doughnuts puff up because yeast in the dough makes tiny bubbles of gas.
jelly-doughnut-coloring-page.colorTips: Golden brown works for the doughnuts, with the little sugar dots left white or colored lightly. Make the jelly peeking out red or purple, and decorate the plate with a blue rim or pattern. Older kids can add a striped napkin under the plate or draw a fourth doughnut.
jelly-doughnut-coloring-page.learning: Counting three doughnuts, then talking about how to share them fairly among family members, is early math in a real-life setting.

latkes-coloring-page.talkAbout: Latkes are crispy potato pancakes fried in oil, a classic food on Hanukkah. Families often eat them with applesauce, sour cream, or both. Ask your child which topping they would pick and whether they'd like to help grate potatoes next time you cook. Potatoes grow underground, and the part we eat is called a tuber.
latkes-coloring-page.colorTips: Golden yellow and light brown make the latkes look crispy, with a darker brown along the lacy edges. Color the applesauce pale yellow or light tan, and give the bowl and spoon their own bright colors. Older kids can draw a little pattern on the plate's rim, like stripes or a ring of small stars.
latkes-coloring-page.learning: Counting the latkes in the stack from bottom to top introduces words like first, second, and third. Count the spoon and the bowl too, so your child can say how many things are on the plate altogether.

hanukkah-gelt-coloring-page.talkAbout: Gelt is a Yiddish word for money, and on Hanukkah many children receive chocolate coins wrapped in gold or silver foil. The coins are often used as playing pieces in the dreidel game. Talk about how real coins look and feel different from one another. Some families also give small amounts of real money as Hanukkah gelt.
hanukkah-gelt-coloring-page.colorTips: Alternate gold and silver on the coins so the pile shines, using yellow and gray if you don't have metallic crayons. The mesh bag can be blue, red, or white, and older kids can color every other diamond in the net. Older kids can draw a design on the face of each coin, like a star or a menorah.
hanukkah-gelt-coloring-page.learning: Counting the coins spilled on the table and sorting them into gold and silver groups mixes counting with sorting.

oil-jug-coloring-page.talkAbout: This little jar of oil connects to the Hanukkah story: when the Temple in Jerusalem was rededicated, a tiny amount of oil burned for eight nights. That's one reason Hanukkah is known as the Festival of Lights. Talk about other ways people use light to celebrate during the dark winter months. Olive oil comes from pressing olives, which grow on trees.
oil-jug-coloring-page.colorTips: A warm clay color like orange-brown or terra cotta works for the jar, with a different color on the stripe around its middle. Make the flame yellow and orange, and color the light rays bright yellow so the whole page glows.
oil-jug-coloring-page.learning: Talking about what happened first, next, and at the end of the oil story is a simple way to practice retelling in order. Counting eight nights on your fingers adds a bit of math to the retelling.

happy-hanukkah-coloring-page.talkAbout: Hanukkah lasts eight nights, and its dates shift from year to year because they follow the Hebrew calendar, usually landing in November or December. Look together at the menorah and dreidel under the words. Ask your child which part of Hanukkah they look forward to most, from lighting candles to eating latkes. Families often sing songs, play games, and give small gifts during the holiday.
happy-hanukkah-coloring-page.colorTips: Blue and white bubble letters look festive, or kids can alternate colors letter by letter. The menorah below can be gold with yellow flames, and the dreidel can match the letters above. Kids who want a challenge can draw Hebrew letters on the dreidel's faces after looking up what they look like together.
happy-hanukkah-coloring-page.learning: Hanukkah has two Ks and two As, so finding the double letters and counting all the letters together is great letter practice. Counting the candles on the small menorah adds one more number job.

easy-apple-coloring-page.talkAbout: Apples grow on trees, start as blossoms in the spring, and ripen in late summer and fall. They come in many colors, from red to green to yellow. If you cut an apple across the middle, the seeds make a little star shape, which is a fun surprise to try at snack time. A grown-up apple tree can grow many apples in one season.
easy-apple-coloring-page.colorTips: Red, green, or yellow all work, so let your child pick their favorite kind of apple. The stem is brown and the leaf is green, and that's all this page needs. Big shapes like this are perfect for chunky crayons or dot markers.
easy-apple-coloring-page.learning: Apple starts with A, the short A sound in ant and alligator, so say it together while coloring. The round shape of the apple is great for practicing coloring in a circle.

easy-sun-coloring-page.talkAbout: The sun is a star, the closest star to Earth, and it gives us light and warmth. It looks small in the sky because it is very far away. Talk about what the sun helps do every day, like growing plants and drying puddles, and remind kids never to look straight at it. Plants use sunlight to make their own food, which is why they turn toward a sunny window.
easy-sun-coloring-page.colorTips: Yellow for the face and orange for the triangle rays is a simple, bright choice. For a pattern, alternate yellow and orange rays all the way around. Little ones can stay inside the big circle, which is large enough for a whole fist grip.
easy-sun-coloring-page.learning: The rays are triangles and the face is a circle, so name both shapes and count the rays together.

easy-balloon-coloring-page.talkAbout: Balloons float when they're filled with helium, a gas that is lighter than air. Balloons blown up with your own breath don't float, which is why they drift down to the floor. Talk about parties or celebrations where your child has seen balloons. If you rub a balloon on your hair, it can stick to a wall, a fun experiment to try at home.
easy-balloon-coloring-page.colorTips: Choose one color for each balloon, like red, blue, and yellow, then color the curly strings to match. This page is perfect for practicing color names, and the big round shapes are easy to fill with crayons or markers. The curly strings are good practice for tracing loops with a pencil before coloring.
easy-balloon-coloring-page.learning: Counting three balloons and naming each color builds number sense and color words at the same time.

easy-fish-coloring-page.talkAbout: Fish breathe underwater using gills, and they swim by moving their tails back and forth. Some fish live in salty oceans and others live in freshwater lakes and rivers. Point to the bubbles floating up and talk about why fish need water to live. A goldfish can live for many years with good care.
easy-fish-coloring-page.colorTips: Orange like a goldfish is a classic choice, but a rainbow fish with a different color on each fin is fun too. Color the bubbles light blue, and leave the shiny spot in the eye white. Older kids can draw scales on the body in a pattern of little curves.
easy-fish-coloring-page.learning: Fish starts with F, a soft, breathy sound, so practice it together and think of other F words like fin and fun. The round body and the triangle tail are shapes to name before coloring.

easy-star-coloring-page.talkAbout: Stars in the night sky are giant balls of hot, glowing gas, very far away. They look tiny and twinkly from Earth because of that distance. This star has a happy face, so talk about what feelings your child's star might have and draw another face on the back. The sun is a star too, just much closer to us than the others.
easy-star-coloring-page.colorTips: Yellow or gold is classic, but any color works on a happy star. Older kids can color each of the five points a different color and leave the face plain so it stands out. A pale blue or purple background makes the star pop.
easy-star-coloring-page.learning: Counting the five points of the star is a great way to practice counting to five. Tracing each point with a finger, up and down, is a nice warm-up for drawing zigzag lines.

easy-house-coloring-page.talkAbout: Houses come in many shapes and sizes, and people live in apartments, trailers, farmhouses, and more. Talk about what your home looks like, including the color of your door. Ask who lives in this little house and make up a short story about them. Some houses are made of wood, others of brick or stone.
easy-house-coloring-page.colorTips: Let your child color the house to look like your own, from the roof to the front door. The windows can be light blue for glass, and the round bush can be green with a few red berry dots. Add a path from the door to the edge of the page with a crayon.
easy-house-coloring-page.learning: This page has a triangle roof, a rectangle door, and square windows, which makes it perfect for naming shapes. Counting the panes in each window adds a small counting job.

easy-butterfly-coloring-page.talkAbout: Butterflies start out as caterpillars, then make a chrysalis, and come out with wings. They taste with their feet and drink nectar from flowers using a long, curly tongue. Look for butterflies in a garden or park and talk about the colors you see. Some butterflies travel long distances, like monarchs, which fly south for the winter.
easy-butterfly-coloring-page.colorTips: Butterfly wings match on both sides, so color the top two wings alike and the bottom two wings alike. The circles inside each wing are perfect for a bright contrasting color. Use a dark color for the body and antennae so the wings stand out. Dot markers fit neatly inside the four circles for the youngest colorists.
easy-butterfly-coloring-page.learning: Making the left and right wings match is an easy introduction to symmetry and matching. Count the four wings, the four circles, and the two antennae.

easy-puppy-coloring-page.talkAbout: Puppies are baby dogs, and they sleep a lot while they grow. Dogs wag their tails for lots of reasons, often when they're happy or excited. Talk about dogs your child knows and what kind of care a puppy needs, like food, water, walks, and lots of love.
easy-puppy-coloring-page.colorTips: Brown, tan, black, or white all suit a puppy, and kids can add spots or patches to make it their own. Color the nose black and the tongue pink, and add a collar with a bright tag. Older kids can draw a bowl or a ball next to the puppy and color that too.
easy-puppy-coloring-page.learning: Puppy has two Ps, so say the P sound together and listen for it at the start and in the middle of the word. Clapping the two beats in pup-py helps kids hear syllables.

race-car-coloring-page.talkAbout: Race cars are built low to the ground so air flows over them smoothly and they grip the track. The wing on the back, called a spoiler, helps push the car down so it stays steady at high speed. Talk about which number your child would paint on their race car and why. Race car drivers wear helmets and fireproof suits to stay safe.
race-car-coloring-page.colorTips: Pick a bright main color and a second color for racing stripes. Use the big circle on the side for a number, and color the speed lines in gray or a light version of the car's color. Older kids can add sponsor logos or a checkered flag.
race-car-coloring-page.learning: Writing a number in the circle on the side, maybe their age, turns this page into number writing practice.

fire-truck-coloring-page.talkAbout: Fire trucks carry ladders, hoses, and tools that firefighters use to put out fires and help people. The long ladder on top can reach high windows. Talk about what your child should do if they hear a fire alarm, and listen together for the sound of a siren. Firefighters also visit schools to teach fire safety.
fire-truck-coloring-page.colorTips: Red is classic, but some fire trucks are actually yellow or lime green, so either is correct. Make the flashing light red or yellow, and color the hose reel gray or black. Older kids can add a firefighter on the ladder or a hose spraying water.
fire-truck-coloring-page.learning: Fire starts with F, so make the soft F sound together and name other F words in the picture, like flashing and front. Counting the wheels and the rungs on the ladder gives kids two quick numbers to find.

dump-truck-coloring-page.talkAbout: Dump trucks carry heavy loads like dirt, sand, and rocks to building sites. The back, called the bed, tips up to pour everything out at once. Watch for dump trucks around town and talk about what they might be carrying. The biggest dump trucks work in mines and have tires taller than a grown-up.
dump-truck-coloring-page.colorTips: Yellow or orange is the classic dump truck look, with black tires and gray rocks. Older kids can color each rock in a slightly different shade of gray and brown so the pile looks real. The tires can be dark gray with light gray hubs, and the cab windows light blue.
dump-truck-coloring-page.learning: Counting the rocks in the pile and talking about heavy and light builds math and science words. Ask your child to guess how many rocks there are before counting, then compare the guess with the real number.

police-car-coloring-page.talkAbout: Police officers drive cars with lights and sirens so other drivers know to move aside. The lights on the roof are called a light bar. Talk about how police officers help in the community and what to do if your child ever gets lost. Police officers often visit schools and community events, which is a nice chance to say hello.
police-car-coloring-page.colorTips: Black and white or blue and white are common police car colors. Make the light bar red and blue, and color the star badge on the door gold. Older kids can add a road with a dashed line underneath the car.
police-car-coloring-page.learning: The star on the door has five points, so count them together and name the circle wheels too. The round headlights and wheels are circles, and the windows are close to rectangles, so shape names come up easily.

school-bus-coloring-page.talkAbout: School buses are yellow so they are easy to see from far away. The stop sign arm on the side swings out to tell other drivers to stop while kids get on and off. Talk about bus safety, like waiting for the bus to stop and staying seated. School bus drivers have special training to keep riders safe.
school-bus-coloring-page.colorTips: Yellow for the bus, black for the tires and stripes, and red for the stop sign makes it look real. Older kids can draw faces of friends in the windows. The windows can be light blue for glass, and the bumpers black or silver.
school-bus-coloring-page.learning: Counting the windows along the side is great counting practice. Counting again from the back of the bus to the front checks the first count. Bus starts with B, so practice that sound too.

tractor-coloring-page.talkAbout: Farmers use tractors to pull plows, plant seeds, and haul heavy loads. The big back wheels help the tractor grip soft, muddy ground. Talk about foods that grow on farms and how a tractor helps get them from the field to the table. Some tractors have tracks instead of wheels to move through very soft ground. Ask your child what they would grow on their own farm if they had a tractor like this one.
tractor-coloring-page.colorTips: Green or red with yellow wheels are popular tractor colors. Color the field green or brown, and add a blue sky behind it. Older kids can add rows of crops or a red barn in the background.
tractor-coloring-page.learning: Comparing the huge back wheel with the small front wheel is a natural way to practice big and small. Count the bolts on the big wheel.

monster-truck-coloring-page.talkAbout: Monster trucks have giant tires that let them climb over and jump off big ramps. People go to shows to watch them do tricks and crush old cars. Talk about how the big tires and springs help soften the landing. Drivers wear helmets and sit strapped into a strong seat for every jump.
monster-truck-coloring-page.colorTips: Bold colors like lime green, purple, or fire red look great on a monster truck. Make the tires black, and color the dust clouds tan or light brown. Older kids can add flames or stripes to the side of the truck. The deep tread on the giant tires is great for careful coloring with a dark gray or black crayon.
monster-truck-coloring-page.learning: Talking about the truck going up the ramp, into the air, and down again builds position words. Count the tires and talk about what the springs do.

garbage-truck-coloring-page.talkAbout: Garbage trucks pick up trash and take it to a place where it can be sorted or disposed of. Many trucks have an arm that lifts and dumps the can automatically. Talk about recycling, and sort a few clean items at home into trash and recycling. Garbage collectors work early in the morning, often before most people wake up.
garbage-truck-coloring-page.colorTips: Green, white, and blue are common garbage truck colors. Color the trash can a different color from the truck, and make the lifting arm gray or black. Older kids can add a few bags of trash or a recycling bin nearby.
garbage-truck-coloring-page.learning: Sorting real objects into trash and recycling after coloring connects the picture to early sorting and grouping skills. Counting the wheels on the long truck and comparing that number with a car's four wheels adds a bit of math.

fireworks-coloring-page.talkAbout: Fireworks get their colors from different metal powders and salts packed inside them, which glow in different colors when they burn. Many cities set off fireworks at midnight to welcome the new year. Talk about how fireworks sound and look, and whether your child likes the booms or prefers watching from far away. Fireworks are for grown-ups to handle, so watching from a safe distance is part of the fun.
fireworks-coloring-page.colorTips: Make each burst a different color, like red, blue, and gold, and color the sky dark blue or purple with crayon so the bursts stand out. The little rooftops below can be cozy browns and grays with yellow light in the windows.
fireworks-coloring-page.learning: Counting the three big bursts and the tiny stars scattered around them gives kids two different counting jobs on one page.

party-hats-coloring-page.talkAbout: Party hats are shaped like cones, a shape kids also see in ice cream cones and traffic cones. A party horn, sometimes called a blowout, uncurls with a toot when you blow into it. Ask your child what makes a celebration feel special to them, from music to staying up late. Some families make their own party hats out of paper.
party-hats-coloring-page.colorTips: One hat has polka dots and one has stripes, so color the dots in a rainbow and the stripes in two alternating colors. The pom-poms on top look fun in bright pink or gold, and the streamers can be every color in the box.
party-hats-coloring-page.learning: Finding the dotted hat and the striped hat, then naming the cone shape, builds pattern and shape vocabulary together. Counting the polka dots on one hat makes a calm counting job for a party day.

midnight-clock-coloring-page.talkAbout: Midnight is 12 o'clock at night, and it's the moment one year ends and the next begins. Both hands on this clock point straight up to the 12. Talk about the difference between the short hour hand and the long minute hand, even if your child isn't ready to read a clock yet. Some families count down the last ten seconds before midnight together.
midnight-clock-coloring-page.colorTips: Give the numbers bright colors and keep the clock face pale so they're easy to read. The stars in each corner can be gold or silver, and the outer ring of the clock can be any bold color. Give the two hands different colors so the short hour hand and long minute hand are easy to tell apart.
midnight-clock-coloring-page.learning: Pointing to each number from 1 to 12 in order and saying them aloud is counting practice with numerals kids see every day.

happy-new-year-2027-coloring-page.talkAbout: The new year starts on January 1 on the calendar most of the world uses, and 2027 is the year coming next. Talk about how old your child will be in 2027 and what they're excited to learn or try. Confetti is made of tiny pieces of paper, so the scattered shapes around the words are a fun detail to point out.
happy-new-year-2027-coloring-page.colorTips: Color each digit of 2027 a different color, or fill the whole number with stripes. The confetti pieces and stars are tiny, so they are a good challenge for older kids with fine-tip markers. Leave a little white inside each letter for a shiny effect.
happy-new-year-2027-coloring-page.learning: Reading the numbers 2, 0, 2, 7 one at a time, then finding the 2 that appears twice, is a quick lesson in number recognition.

new-year-balloons-coloring-page.talkAbout: This bunch has five balloons, and one is shaped like a star. Balloons come in many shapes besides round, from hearts to numbers. Ask your child how they would celebrate the new year if they could plan the party, from the snacks to the music. Ask your child which balloon they would hold onto at midnight.
new-year-balloons-coloring-page.colorTips: Make every balloon its own color, and the star balloon gold or silver so it stands out in the middle. Leave the shine marks on each balloon white to make them look glossy, and color the confetti in bright dots. Tie the ribbons together at the bottom in one bright color.
new-year-balloons-coloring-page.learning: Counting the round balloons, then the star, and adding them together is an early addition problem kids can see. Comparing the round balloons with the star balloon also gives kids a chance to name both shapes.

new-year-bear-coloring-page.talkAbout: This teddy bear is ready to celebrate with a party hat, a balloon, and a party horn. Many families stay home on New Year's Eve and celebrate early, which suits little ones who can't stay up until midnight. Ask your child how they would like to celebrate this year. Talk about one fun thing your child did this past year that the bear could celebrate with them.
new-year-bear-coloring-page.colorTips: Brown or honey colored fur with a lighter tummy and muzzle looks cuddly. The polka dots on the hat can be a rainbow, and the balloon can be your child's favorite color. Older kids can draw confetti around the bear.
new-year-bear-coloring-page.learning: Talking about the bear's hat, balloon, and horn practices position words like on top of, in his hand, and in his mouth.

new-year-goals-coloring-page.talkAbout: A goal is something you want to do or get better at. This page has three big stars, so your child can choose three goals for the new year, like learning to ride a bike, writing their name, or helping feed the dog. Keep goals small and doable, and celebrate progress along the way. Hang the finished page where your child can see it, and check in on their goals each month.
new-year-goals-coloring-page.colorTips: Have your child draw or write one goal inside each star before coloring around it. The bubble letters at the top can be filled with a bright color, and each star can be outlined in a different color.
new-year-goals-coloring-page.learning: Writing or dictating a goal inside each star builds early writing skills and gives kids practice putting their ideas into words.

countdown-rocket-coloring-page.talkAbout: Rockets count down before launch, and people count down to midnight on New Year's Eve, so this page connects the two. Real rockets push hot gases out of the bottom to blast off upward. Practice counting down together from 10, then shout blast off at the end. Astronauts ride rockets into space, and some live on the International Space Station.
countdown-rocket-coloring-page.colorTips: Make the rocket silver, red, or white with a bright window, and the flames orange and yellow. Color the numbers 3, 2, 1 in three different colors, and fill the smoke clouds with soft gray. Older kids can add stars and planets in the background.
countdown-rocket-coloring-page.learning: Counting backward from 3 to 1, then from 10 to 1, is a fun way to practice counting in reverse order. Tracing the 3, 2, and 1 with a finger before coloring adds number formation practice.

big-heart-coloring-page.talkAbout: The heart shape stands for love and caring, even though a real heart looks quite different. Your real heart is a muscle about the size of your fist, and it pumps blood all around your body day and night, even while you sleep. Have your child put a hand on their chest to feel the beat, do ten jumping jacks, and notice how it speeds up.
big-heart-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the big center heart red, pink, or purple, then give each of the six small hearts its own color.
