Older kids can fill the big heart with stripes, zigzags, or tiny hearts, and the extra thick outline makes this one of the easiest pages for toddlers using chunky crayons.
big-heart-coloring-page.learning: Counting the six small hearts, then pointing to the big one and the little ones, mixes counting with size words like big, small, biggest, and smallest.

valentine-teddy-bear-coloring-page.talkAbout: Teddy bears got their name from Theodore Roosevelt, a U.S. president whose nickname was Teddy. This bear is hugging a big heart, a sweet picture for a card to a grandparent or friend. Ask your child who they would give a big hug to on Valentine's Day and why that person is special to them.
valentine-teddy-bear-coloring-page.colorTips: Brown, honey, or even pink fur suits this bear, with a lighter shade on the ears, muzzle, and round paw pads. Make the heart bright red or pink so it stands out, and older kids can add a bow tie or tiny hearts on the bear's feet.
valentine-teddy-bear-coloring-page.learning: Writing a family member's name inside the big heart before coloring turns this page into gentle name-writing practice with a real reason behind it. Count the bear's round ears and paws to add a quick counting job.

valentine-puppy-coloring-page.talkAbout: This puppy holds a heart balloon string in its mouth and sits beside a small wrapped gift. Dogs show love in their own ways, like wagging their tails, leaning against you, and following you from room to room. Talk about how your child shows love to the people and pets in their life, and how they can tell when someone feels loved.
valentine-puppy-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the puppy in any dog color your child likes, from golden to spotted black and white, with pink inside the ears. Make the heart balloon red or pink, and wrap the gift box in a bright color with a different color for the bow and ribbon.
valentine-puppy-coloring-page.learning: Puppy starts with P, so practice the popping P sound together and look for more P words around the page, like present, pink, and paws.

valentine-dinosaur-coloring-page.talkAbout: This friendly T. rex is holding a big heart in its short arms. Real T. rex arms were small compared with its huge body, but they were strong. Scientists who dig up and study dinosaur fossils are called paleontologists, a big word kids enjoy saying. Ask your child to invent a silly dinosaur valentine message, like "You're dino-mite."
valentine-dinosaur-coloring-page.colorTips: Green, purple, or orange all look great on this dinosaur, and the round spots on its body and tail can be a second color. Make the heart red or pink so it pops against the body, and color the striped belly a lighter shade.
valentine-dinosaur-coloring-page.learning: Counting the spots, then counting the pointed teeth in that big smile, gives kids two quick counting jobs on one page. Clapping the three beats in di-no-saur adds a quick syllable game.

valentine-unicorn-coloring-page.talkAbout: Unicorns are imaginary animals from old stories, usually shown as a horse with one spiral horn. This one has a heart on its side and stands on a fluffy cloud with hearts floating around it. Ask your child to make up a short story about where this unicorn flies on Valentine's Day and who it visits.
valentine-unicorn-coloring-page.colorTips: Pastel colors like pink, lavender, and light blue look lovely on the wavy mane and tail, and you can repeat them in the floating hearts. Make the heart on its side bright red, the horn gold or silver, and leave the cloud white with a soft gray edge. Older kids can add a few sparkles around the horn.
valentine-unicorn-coloring-page.learning: Counting the floating hearts around the unicorn, then finding the one heart that is on the unicorn itself, practices counting and careful looking.

valentine-mailbox-coloring-page.talkAbout: When the little flag on a mailbox is up, it tells the mail carrier there is a letter inside to pick up. Mail carriers bring letters and packages to homes on most days of the week. Talk about making a real valentine and mailing it to a grandparent or friend, then watching for a reply. Point out your own mailbox or building mail slot next time you pass it.
valentine-mailbox-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the mailbox red, blue, or silver, and make the flag a bright contrasting color. The three envelopes can be white, pink, or pale yellow with red hearts, and older kids can write a tiny name on each envelope before they color.
valentine-mailbox-coloring-page.learning: Writing a short note, even just a name and a heart, to tuck into a real envelope connects this page to early writing with a purpose.

be-my-valentine-coloring-page.talkAbout: Valentine's Day falls on February 14, and people share cards, kind notes, and small treats with family and friends. Many classrooms swap valentines, so this page is a nice way to talk about including everyone. Help your child make a list of the people they would like to give a valentine to this year.
be-my-valentine-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the bubble letters red and pink, or alternate colors letter by letter across each word. Fill the big heart frame with a soft background color, and give each little heart floating around it a different shade. Older kids can add stripes or dots inside the letters.
be-my-valentine-coloring-page.learning: Hunting for the letters in VALENTINE that also appear in your child's name is a fun letter-matching game, and counting the letters in each word adds a little math.

love-bugs-coloring-page.talkAbout: Ladybugs are small beetles, and many have bright red or orange shells with black spots. When a ladybug flies, it lifts its hard outer shell and unfolds thin wings tucked underneath. Gardeners like them because they eat tiny plant-eating bugs called aphids. Like all insects, a ladybug has six legs.
love-bugs-coloring-page.colorTips: Red shells with pink or black heart-shaped spots look sweet, and the faces can stay a soft black or gray. Color the big leaf in two greens, with the vein lines darker, and add a few small hearts floating above the bugs for a finishing touch.
love-bugs-coloring-page.learning: Counting the heart spots on each ladybug and checking whether both bugs have the same number is an easy counting and comparing task. Counting all the legs on both bugs together is a fun step up for older kids.

shamrock-coloring-page.talkAbout: A shamrock is a young three-leaf clover and a well-known symbol of Ireland. St. Patrick's Day is on March 17, and many people wear green or a shamrock pin to celebrate. On your next walk, look for clover in the grass and count the leaves on a few plants together.
shamrock-coloring-page.colorTips: Use several shades of green, making the big shamrock the darkest and the small ones around it lighter. Older kids can draw vein lines inside each leaf and color them a deeper green, or fill the background with a simple stripe pattern.
shamrock-coloring-page.learning: Counting three leaves on every shamrock, then counting the shamrocks themselves, gives kids lots of practice with the number three and the number four. Shamrock starts with the SH sound, the quiet sound we make to ask for hush.

four-leaf-clover-coloring-page.talkAbout: Most clovers have three leaves, so finding one with four is rare and is often called lucky. The leaves on this clover are shaped like little hearts. Clover plants also grow small round flowers, usually white or pink, that bees love to visit. Go on a clover hunt in the yard or park and see what you find.
four-leaf-clover-coloring-page.colorTips: Color each leaf a slightly different green, or make all four one bright green with a darker curved stem. For a challenge, older kids can color each leaf with a different pattern, like dots, stripes, swirls, and checks.
four-leaf-clover-coloring-page.learning: Counting the four leaves and noticing that each one is a heart shape builds counting and shape recognition at once. Counting how many more leaves this clover has than a three-leaf one is an easy first subtraction question.

leprechaun-coloring-page.talkAbout: Leprechauns are small, mischievous characters from Irish folklore, often shown with a tall hat, a curly beard, and a pot of gold. In many stories, a leprechaun who gets caught has to grant a wish or give up his gold. Ask your child what they would wish for if they ever caught one.
leprechaun-coloring-page.colorTips: Green for the hat, vest, and pants is the classic look, with an orange or red curly beard. Make the hat buckle and the shining gold coin in his hand bright yellow or gold, and color the shoe buckles to match.
leprechaun-coloring-page.learning: Leprechaun starts with L, so practice the L sound with your tongue behind your teeth and name other L words like lucky, leaf, and lollipop. Counting the buttons on his vest adds a small number job.

pot-of-gold-coloring-page.talkAbout: In Irish stories, a leprechaun hides his pot of gold at the end of a rainbow, where no one can quite reach it. Real gold is a soft, shiny metal that doesn't rust, which is why old gold coins still gleam. Talk about what your child would do with a pot of gold, and whether they would share it.
pot-of-gold-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the round pot black or dark gray and make the coins bright yellow or gold. Older kids can leave a small white spot on each coin so it looks shiny, and the coins on the ground can be colored a slightly darker gold.
pot-of-gold-coloring-page.learning: Counting the coins spilling out of the pot and then the coins on the ground, and adding them together, is a simple first addition problem.

rainbow-coloring-page.talkAbout: Rainbows appear when sunlight shines through raindrops, which split the white light into colors. The colors always show up in the same order, with red on the outside. You can make a small rainbow on a sunny day by spraying a fine mist from a garden hose with the sun behind you. Ask your child to point to where the pot of gold sits and where the cloud sits, at opposite ends.
rainbow-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the six bands in rainbow order from the outside in: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple. Leave the fluffy cloud white or pale gray, and fill the little pot of gold with yellow coins so the page tells the whole leprechaun story.
rainbow-coloring-page.learning: Naming the six rainbow colors in order is great practice for color words and for putting things in sequence. Kids can count the bands after naming them, which should come to six.

leprechaun-hat-coloring-page.talkAbout: This tall hat, with its wide band and big buckle, is the kind leprechauns wear in drawings and stories. Many people wear tall green hats to St. Patrick's Day parades for fun. Ask your child to design their own holiday hat, and what they would tuck into the band instead of a shamrock.
leprechaun-hat-coloring-page.colorTips: Green is classic for the hat, with a black band and a gold buckle. Make the shamrock a lighter or brighter green so it stands out, and older kids can decorate the band with a pattern of tiny shamrocks or stripes.
leprechaun-hat-coloring-page.learning: The buckle is a square, the band is a rectangle, and the brim is a long oval, so name each shape as you color it. Hat is a short word that's easy to sound out, h-a-t.

leprechaun-trap-coloring-page.talkAbout: Building a leprechaun trap is a popular St. Patrick's Day activity in many classrooms and homes. This trap uses a box propped up with a stick, a little ladder, and gold coins as bait. In some families, kids wake up to find the trap knocked over and a few chocolate coins left behind.
leprechaun-trap-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the box brown like cardboard, and make the stick and ladder a wood color. The bait coins can be yellow or gold, and older kids can add green grass, small flowers, or a sign that says GOLD to tempt the leprechaun.
leprechaun-trap-coloring-page.learning: Talking through how the trap works, step by step, introduces early engineering ideas like planning, building, and testing. Counting the rungs on the ladder and the coins in the bait pile adds two counting jobs.

happy-st-patricks-day-coloring-page.talkAbout: St. Patrick's Day honors Saint Patrick, the patron saint of Ireland, and it is celebrated on March 17 with parades, music, and lots of green. Some cities even dye a river green for the day. Ask your child what they would wear to a St. Patrick's Day parade, and look at a map to find Ireland together.
happy-st-patricks-day-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the bubble letters in different shades of green, or alternate green and gold letter by letter. The shamrocks around the edges can be a darker green, and older kids can tuck a tiny rainbow or pot of gold into one corner.
happy-st-patricks-day-coloring-page.learning: Spotting the period in ST. and the apostrophe in PATRICK'S is a quick, hands-on look at what small punctuation marks do. Counting the shamrocks around the edge adds a quick number task.

easter-bunny-coloring-page.talkAbout: The Easter bunny is a character from folklore who brings eggs and treats in the spring. Real rabbits have long ears that help them hear well and stay cool, and they twitch their noses to sniff the air. Talk about how your family celebrates Easter or welcomes spring, from egg hunts to planting seeds.
easter-bunny-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the bunny white, gray, or brown, with pink inside the long ears. The egg it's holding already has zigzags and dots, so pick bright colors for each band, and make the two flowers at its feet any spring colors your child loves.
easter-bunny-coloring-page.learning: Bunny starts with B, so practice the bouncy B sound together and list other B words like basket, blue, and bloom. Counting the bunny's whiskers on each side is a funny counting job kids enjoy.

easter-egg-coloring-page.talkAbout: Decorating eggs is a spring tradition in many countries, and some families pass down special patterns year after year. In some places, people roll eggs down a hill or race them across a lawn. Eggs also link to spring because many birds lay eggs and raise chicks at this time of year.
easter-egg-coloring-page.colorTips: Give each wide band of the egg its own color, then pick contrasting colors for the zigzags and dots. Older kids can repeat a color pattern from top to bottom. When it's done, cut the egg out and hang it in a window as a spring decoration.
easter-egg-coloring-page.learning: Naming the zigzags, dots, and stripes, then repeating the same colors in matching bands, builds early pattern skills that support math. Counting the dots in each row is a quick extra.

easter-basket-coloring-page.talkAbout: Easter baskets are often filled with soft grass, decorated eggs, and small treats. This basket is woven, which means strips are laced over and under each other, the same way rugs, mats, and some fabrics are made. Ask your child what they would put in their own basket besides eggs.
easter-basket-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the basket tan or brown, or alternate two browns across the woven strips for a challenge. Make the grass bright green and the big bow on the handle a spring color. Each of the five eggs has its own pattern, so give each one its own colors too.
easter-basket-coloring-page.learning: Counting the five eggs, then naming which one has stripes, dots, flowers, hearts, or zigzags, mixes counting with describing words. Ask which egg sits in the middle to practice position words.

baby-chick-coloring-page.talkAbout: Chicken eggs usually hatch after about three weeks of being kept warm by a mother hen or an incubator. A new chick is covered in soft, fluffy feathers called down. Point to the cracked eggshell beside this chick and talk about how it pecked its way out. Then name other baby animals born in spring.
baby-chick-coloring-page.colorTips: Yellow is the classic chick color, with orange for the beak and feet. The broken eggshell can be white or light tan, and the tulip and daisies give a chance to use pinks, purples, and greens.
baby-chick-coloring-page.learning: Chick starts with the CH sound, which is two letters making one sound, so practice it together with words like cheese, chair, and chin. Counting the flowers around the chick is a quick bonus job.

easter-egg-hunt-coloring-page.talkAbout: Egg hunts are a favorite Easter activity, with eggs tucked in grass, under bushes, and behind trees. Look at this picture together and find every hidden egg before coloring. Then talk about the best hiding spots in your own yard or home, and who gets to hide the eggs next time.
easter-egg-hunt-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the hidden eggs in the brightest colors you have so they are easy to spot, and keep the grass, bush, and tree in natural greens and browns. Older kids can add patterns to each egg, and the child's cap and shirt can be any color they like.
easter-egg-hunt-coloring-page.learning: Searching for and counting the hidden eggs is a fun visual scanning task, and splitting them into eggs found and eggs still hiding adds a little math.

spring-lamb-coloring-page.talkAbout: Lambs are baby sheep, and many are born in late winter or spring. Sheep live in groups called flocks and spend much of the day eating grass. Their curly wool can be sheared off, usually once a year, and spun into yarn for sweaters, hats, and mittens. Check a sweater label at home to see if it is made of wool.
spring-lamb-coloring-page.colorTips: Leave the curly wool white or color it a soft cream, with a pink or tan face and ears. The daisies can be white with yellow centers, and the meadow can be bright green. Older kids can draw a little fence or a barn in the background.
spring-lamb-coloring-page.learning: Lamb starts with L, so practice the L sound and list other L words like leaf, little, and lily.

easter-cross-lilies-coloring-page.talkAbout: For Christians, Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus, and the cross is a symbol of that story. Easter lilies are large white trumpet-shaped flowers that many churches display at Easter. The sunrise behind the cross is a reminder of early morning Easter services that some families attend. Families who don't celebrate Easter as a religious holiday can still talk about spring flowers and sunrises.
easter-cross-lilies-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the cross a warm wood brown and the lilies white with yellow centers and green leaves. The sunrise rays can fade from yellow near the hill to orange and pink farther out, and the grass on the hill can be a fresh spring green.
easter-cross-lilies-coloring-page.learning: Counting the lilies and then the rays of the sunrise gives kids a calm counting task that fits a quiet Sunday morning.

bunny-painting-eggs-coloring-page.talkAbout: This bunny is busy painting stripes on an egg, with a little paint pot nearby and two finished eggs beside it. Some families dye real eggs with food coloring, and others use natural dyes like onion skins or beets. Ask your child what design they would paint on an egg if they had a brush and a pot of paint.
bunny-painting-eggs-coloring-page.colorTips: Color the paint in the pot the same color as the stripes the bunny is painting, which is a fun little detail to notice. One finished egg has dots and the other has wavy lines, so give those patterns bright contrasting colors.
bunny-painting-eggs-coloring-page.learning: Spotting stripes on one egg, dots on another, and wavy lines on the last builds pattern recognition and describing words. Counting all three eggs, the painted one and the two finished ones, adds a quick number job.
